# Chapter 10 - sketch answers {.unnumbered}

\(1\) Reduce: Add MFA to close R1 - the usual case. Accept: A rare, minor risk
such as brief downtime of the internal wiki - below the line, documented.
Transfer: Cyber-insurance against part of R3's financial loss - hard to reduce
to zero. Avoid: Not storing card numbers at all, leaving them with the payment
provider - the risky activity stops. (2) MFA lowers likelihood - the attack
no longer succeeds with a password alone. Encrypted backups lower impact -
stolen or destroyed data is recoverable and unreadable. Scrubbing lowers
likelihood of a successful flood reaching the checkout. The response plan lowers
impact - the breach still happens, but shorter and smaller. (3) Application
controls run *on* the systems GITC govern: If access and change management are
weak, anyone could alter the code or the data behind the automated check, so its
output proves nothing - hence GITC first. Concrete: Developers with direct
write access to the production database undermine every automated calculation in
the application above it. (4) Bank: A 24/7 SOC with a SIEM and named analysts.
FastGoods: Provider alerting on, anomaly notifications to the two technical
staff, a fifteen-minute weekly dashboard review. Both must pass the same purpose
test: An incident is detected in time to act - alerts to an unread mailbox
fail it. (5) The internal audit of Clause 9 (PDCA Check) finds the three admin
accounts; the finding is a nonconformity, and corrective action (Clause 10, Act)
enforces MFA on them and adds the check to onboarding; the register's R1 row
updates its residual, and the SoA row for A.8.5 keeps its justification - the
same loop as Chapter 3's @exm-pdcaloop, now closed with evidence.
